chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
title: Photographs, sudden fame and its strain
summary: A glamorous photo in November 1939; overnight success was hard on her and she didn't always feel like performing.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Okay. By the way there is one thing. Even though he may have been opposed to you having photographs taken early on, in fact there's an extremely /glamorous photograph of you in Harpers Bazaar, November 1939.

It was by that time no longer a secret. I had already been exposed. I didn't know what was going on and this was a thing I heard through Claude later, that by the time the Archie Winston article broke it was no longer a secret.
This overnight success which led you to Hollywood which we'll come to in a little while, was that a hard thing for you to go through? Apparently it was a big change in your life.
I didn't realize what was happening at all except for the fact that I just found myself busy as all outdoors. I mean, I was being called upon to do benefits and do this, that and the other

and there were times when I didn't feel like doing it but someone says, you know, you have to do this. This is part of the game, you know. All of a sudden I found myself very, very busy. Even when the selection of "Loch Lomond" was cut off the air. I mean, up until that time I don't suppose it made any difference who it was. It was just a swing version that mattered. This Neil Fitzpatrick in Detroit didn't know whether I was white or black, he just didn't like the idea of "Loch Lomond" getting swung.
